intro: I'm {age} and live in Vienna. Most of what I build starts because I need it: a panel to run my own servers, a route planner for my Zivildienst tours, a chartplotter for the boat, two little boards that save me a few annoying seconds every day. Sometimes it's just curiosity, like teaching a Mac to DJ.

projects.name: Venvy
projects.one: My own Heroku, running on a mini PC at home.
projects.why: My favourite, and the one I've put the most time into: more than a year, most of it before it went public. I wanted my own apps online without renting a platform. Everything on ringtwo.win runs on it, including this page.

toy.title: Break a deploy
toy.hint: Ship a broken release and watch Venvy notice and roll it back.

story: You upload an app or point Venvy at a git repo, and it runs it, watches it and gives it a public hostname. It handles Python, Node, Bun, Deno, Go, Rust, PHP, Ruby, Java and static sites, and each app runs as its own Unix user, so one compromised app can't read another one's files.

A deploy pulls, installs, builds, restarts and then checks the app actually answers. If it doesn't, the previous release comes back on its own, which is what you just did above. Every deploy stays in the history, so you can roll back to it later.

Venvy updates itself with the same caution. A new version is checked against its signature, installed next to the running one, and the database is snapshotted first. If the new version doesn't come up healthy, the installer switches back.
details: Browser terminal, live logs, cron jobs, CPU and memory alerts.
Backups to S3, WebDAV or scp on a schedule.
Push-to-deploy webhooks from GitHub, GitLab, Gitea and Forgejo.
A strict CSP with no inline script, and a per-origin key so hosted apps can't ride the panel's session cookie.

items: An app's terminal, running as that app's own Unix user.
Every deploy is a release you can roll back to.

projects.name: Passable
projects.one: Give it songs, get back one continuous mix, built stem by stem.
projects.why: I wanted to know how hard it really is to automate what a DJ does. Very, it turns out: you need stem separation, beat tracking, key detection, and a detector for when a singer breathes.

toy.title: Listen to a transition
toy.hint: Two real transitions Passable planned on its own. Watch A hand over to B.

story: Every song is split into vocals, melody, drums and bass on Core ML: HTDemucs v4 for the band, Mel-Band RoFormer for the voice. Then Passable finds the beat, the key, the song's structure, and where each vocal line starts and ends.

Voices hand over between lines, on a breath. On-device speech recognition gets the words wrong but the timing roughly right. Snapping that timing to a map of the singer's breaths makes the cut land between words.

A real drummer drifts a percent or two from bar to bar, so each bar is stretched to the average tempo and keeps its feel. During a set, requests get downloaded, separated and mixed in without the music stopping.
details: The set is ordered by tempo, key and energy, building toward its hardest song.
B's chorus or drop is placed to land as A leaves.
One kick and one bass line at a time. The low end swaps on a single downbeat.
Renders sample-exact to AAC or 24-bit WAV, or sends the set to the iPhone app.

items: Transition 9 → 10 of a 59-song set, untouched. A's voice leaves at the end of its line, the melodies swap, and kick and bass change hands on one downbeat.
The set, ordered, with what each transition does.

projects.name: EAR Router
projects.one: The route planner I use on every Meals on Wheels tour of my Zivildienst.
projects.why: I'm doing my Zivildienst driving Essen auf Rädern in Vienna, and this is the app on my phone every tour. Almost every feature started as something that slowed me down on the road.

toy.title: Find the door
toy.hint: Type an address the way delivery lists write it. The app's own rules find the exact entrance in the city's register, live.

facts: commits, the most of anything here
story: Delivery lists write Viennese addresses every way there is: Gentzgasse 129/1/2/23, Großfeldstraße 9/Parz.68, umlauts typed as “oe”, streets glued to their numbers. The app splits off the Stiege or garden plot, which Vienna's register files as an address of its own with its own front door. It drops the Tür and Stock, which no register knows, and asks the city. You just watched that happen.

An answer is only taken if it's in the right district, on the right street and at the right door. Otherwise the pin goes on the map as “≈” so I check it, instead of looking confident and being wrong. If every answer agrees the address is in another district, the app offers to move it. The stop order then comes from my own OSRM server on the mini PC, and arrival times from the pace I've actually kept that day, a model I backtested against 12 real tours.
I tap Geliefert at the door, in the stairwell, not where the van is parked. So the app learns door time rather than parking time, and remembers which floor every customer lives on.
details: A preflight checklist runs in the yard, while every failure is still cheap.
Hands the next stop to Apple Maps, Waze or Google Maps with the building's actual entrance.
CarPlay, and a read-only “Hey Siri, nächster Stopp”.
The whole store backs up to one readable JSON file, because everything lives on one phone.

items: The stop to drive to now.

projects.name: Leeway
projects.one: A chartplotter that plans passages around rocks, shallows and bad wind.
projects.why: I go boating, and I wanted a plotter that thinks about depth, wind and rocks the way I do when I plan a passage. The first version took five days.

toy.title: Sail around the rocks
toy.hint: Drag A and B. Change the draft and the wind. The route only goes where the boat floats.

story: Shortest finds the shortest path through water deeper than the boat's draft plus a margin. It stays clear of charted rocks, wrecks, obstructions and cardinal marks, and away from bridges lower than the mast.
Fastest grows isochrones through the forecast wind using the boat's own polar, and tacks where it pays. The toy above runs a much smaller version of both on a made-up archipelago.

Underway it has an AIS collision alarm, an anchor watch, man overboard, and NMEA instruments over the boat's Wi-Fi, and alarms sound even with the phone on silent. The charts come from open bathymetry and official Croatian data, and a Rust / axum server on the same mini PC as this page serves them.
details: Day, dusk and night palettes, switched by the sun.
Light sectors with their characteristics, e.g. Fl(2)R.5s 12m 6M.
Tap anything for the object, its depth, and the bearing and distance from the boat.
Polars can be imported straight from designers' tables or ORC certificates.

items: A weather-routed passage through the Kvarner.
The Kornati, with seamarks and soundings.

projects.name: garageDoor-pro
projects.one: A box in the car that opens the garage door when I leave and when I come home.
projects.why: I was tired of fishing for the garage remote every time I drove in or out. Now a GPS and one transistor do it.

toy.title: Drive home
toy.hint: Drive away and back. The state machine follows the firmware's rules, four times faster.

story: An ESP32-C3 and a GPS module press the button of a spare remote through one transistor. It runs off the car's USB, so it boots with the ignition and loses power when I park.

The garage is underground and has no GPS reception, so the board remembers in flash where it was parked. At boot it already knows it's driving out. That's the 10 presses you saw before the GPS even had a fix.

There are two radii because GPS jitters at the edge: arriving counts at 150 m, leaving at 300 m, so the state can't flap. The state machine is pure C, unit-tested on the host under AddressSanitizer and UBSan. The 4-layer board is generated from a Python netlist.
details: A fix only counts with gnssFixOK, at most 50 m accuracy and at least 4 satellites.
A captive-portal web panel sets home once, and the radii are configurable there.
OTA updates, LED status codes, and a perfboard version you can build in about an hour.

items: garageDoor-pro v1.1: ESP32-C3-MINI-1 on four layers.

projects.name: dji-fcc-esp32
projects.one: A pocket dongle that does the job of a phone app.
projects.why: I didn't want to plug a phone into the drone remote and run an app every single time. Now it's a dongle with one LED.

toy.title: Patch a remote
toy.hint: Plug the dongle in, once with Espressif's stock USB stack and once with mine.

story: The ESP32-S3 runs as a USB host, finds the remote's serial interface, sends two packets, and shows the result on an LED. The patch has to be repeated every time the drone and remote power up, which is exactly why a phone app was so annoying.

Full-speed USB allows bulk packets of at most 64 bytes. The remote announces 512 anyway, and Espressif's USB host stack refuses it. So the project ships a patched copy of that stack, with the check relaxed and the transmit FIFO sized to fit.

The battery board is generated from one Python source and comes with Gerbers, BOM, placement and a STEP model. A Web Serial flasher on GitHub Pages flashes it straight from Chrome, and CI redeploys it on every push.
details: The two packets come from DJI-FCC-HACK. This replaces its Android app.
Tested on a real remote with a dev board. The custom board hasn't been assembled yet.
FCC power is only legal in the US. Power-cycling goes back to CE.

items: Rev A, 80 × 34 mm, battery and USB-C.
